lead: A summing amplifier adds several voltages into one output. The inverting summer sends each input through its own resistor to a virtual ground, so their currents add and one feedback resistor turns the total back into a voltage. A difference amplifier subtracts one input from another using four resistors. These circuits mix audio, shift voltage levels, read bridge sensors and remove offsets. The key is the resistor matching condition; resistor tolerance sets the real rejection.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 (virtual ground and ideal op-amp), Chapter 6.2 (inverting and non-inverting gains), and superposition from basic circuit theory.

sections.h3: Inverting summer: currents add at a virtual ground

blocks.text: The inverting summer has n inputs v₁ to vₙ, each through its own resistor R₁ to Rₙ to the inverting input. The non-inverting input is grounded. The feedback resistor R_f returns the output to the inverting input. Negative feedback holds the inverting node at 0 V, a virtual ground (Chapter 6.1). The op-amp input draws no current, so all input current flows through R_f.
Each input current is i_k = v_k/R_k. KCL at the virtual ground gives Σ i_k + v_out/R_f = 0, so:

blocks.where: R_f is the feedback resistor in ohms; R_k and v_k are the k-th input resistor in ohms and input voltage in volts; v_out is the output in volts.

blocks.text: This is a weighted sum: a large v_k or a small R_k gives a large contribution. With equal input resistors R, the output is −(R_f/R)(v₁ + … + vₙ). Set R_f = R/n to get the negative average. Set binary weights, such as R, R/2 and R/4, to make a simple DAC; see Unit 7 for full DAC design.

A non-inverting summer feeds the inputs through resistors to the non-inverting input. A resistor R_g from that node to ground and the feedback divider R_f, R₁ set the gain. Superposition gives v₊ = (Σ v_k/R_k)/(Σ 1/R_k + 1/R_g) and v_out = (1 + R_f/R₁)v₊. Most designers choose the inverting summer because its summing node is a true 0 V virtual ground. The op-amp inputs then see no common-mode voltage. The non-inverting summer has a signal-dependent common-mode voltage and needs matched resistors.

The subtractor uses four resistors. v₁ drives R₁ to the inverting input; R_f feeds back from the output to that node. v₂ drives R₂ to the non-inverting input; R₃ goes from that node to ground. Derive by superposition.

items: Set v₂ = 0. The non-inverting node is at 0 V. The circuit is an inverting amplifier: v_out1 = −(R_f/R₁)v₁.
Set v₁ = 0. The non-inverting node is v₊ = v₂R₃/(R₂ + R₃). The gain to the output is 1 + R_f/R₁, so v_out2 = (1 + R_f/R₁)v₂R₃/(R₂ + R₃).
Add the outputs. If R₃/R₂ = R_f/R₁ = k, then R₃/(R₂ + R₃) = k/(1 + k) and 1 + R_f/R₁ = 1 + k. The product is k, so v_out = k(v₂ − v₁).

blocks.where: R_f, R₁, R₂ and R₃ are in ohms; v₁, v₂ and v_out are in volts. The ratio condition makes the common-mode terms cancel.

blocks.text: The subtractor removes a common voltage only when its resistor ratios match. Let t be the fractional tolerance, for example t = 0.01 for 1 % resistors. Mismatch makes the common-mode gain nonzero. A useful worst-case estimate is CMRR ≈ 1/(4t). For 1 % resistors, CMRR ≈ 1/(4 × 0.01) = 25, which is 20 log₁₀ 25 ≈ 28 dB. That is poor when a small signal sits on a large common-mode voltage.

blocks.where: t is fractional tolerance (0.01 for 1 %); CMRR is differential gain divided by common-mode gain; CMRR_dB is that ratio in decibels.

blocks.text: Trim one resistor or use a matched network for exact ratios. In a bridge measurement, the subtractor keeps the small difference between the two bridge outputs. In a sensor circuit, it removes a fixed offset before the ADC. Audio mixers use the inverting summer to add channels. Level shifting adds or subtracts a DC voltage. In the subtractor the op-amp offset voltage appears at the output multiplied by the noise gain 1 + R_f/R₁. In an n-input inverting summer the same offset is multiplied by 1 + R_f/R_eq, where R_eq = R₁∥R₂∥…∥Rₙ, so keep R_f no larger than needed. Neither gain is the signal gain.

figure.caption: Three input voltages become currents through their resistors, add at the 0 V virtual ground, and the total flows through R_f to make a negative output. The values are those of the worked example.

spec.title: Three-input inverting summer
spec.aria: Three input voltages become currents through R₁, R₂ and R₃, add at the virtual ground, and the total flows through R_f to the output.

examples.question: An inverting summer has R_f = 10 kΩ with v₁ = 1 V through R₁ = 10 kΩ, v₂ = 0.5 V through R₂ = 20 kΩ, and v₃ = 0.2 V through R₃ = 4 kΩ. Find v_out. Next, a subtractor has R₁ = R₂ = R₃ = R_f = 10 kΩ, v₁ = 2 V at the inverting input and v₂ = 1.5 V at the non-inverting input; find v_out.
steps: The inverting input is a virtual ground at 0 V. The input currents are i₁ = 1 V / 10 kΩ = 100 µA, i₂ = 0.5 V / 20 kΩ = 25 µA, and i₃ = 0.2 V / 4 kΩ = 50 µA.
All three currents flow into the virtual ground, so the total current through R_f is i_f = 100 µA + 25 µA + 50 µA = 175 µA.
The output is v_out = −i_f R_f = −175 µA × 10 kΩ = −1.75 V.
For the subtractor, the resistor ratios match: R₃/R₂ = 1 and R_f/R₁ = 1. Use v_out = (R_f/R₁)(v₂ − v₁) = 1 × (1.5 V − 2 V) = −0.5 V.
examples.answer: The inverting summer output is −1.75 V, and the subtractor output is −0.5 V.

traps: Dropping the minus sign in an inverting summer. All currents enter the virtual ground, so the output is negative when the inputs are positive.
Thinking equal input resistors alone give the average. You also need R_f = R/n to get −(average).
Assuming a difference amplifier rejects common-mode perfectly. It does so only when R₃/R₂ = R_f/R₁. With 1 % resistors the worst-case CMRR is about 25, or 28 dB.
Using k(v₂ − v₁) for a subtractor without checking the ratio condition. If the four resistors are not matched, a common-mode input also produces an output.
Forgetting that op-amp offset voltage is amplified by the noise gain of the circuit (1 + R_f/R₁ for the subtractor, 1 + R_f/R_eq for the summer), not by its signal gain.

quiz.q: In an inverting summer, what voltage is held at the inverting input, and why?
quiz.a: 0 V, a virtual ground. Negative feedback and high open-loop gain force v₋ = v₊ = 0 V, and the op-amp input current is zero.

quiz.q: Why does an inverting summer with equal input resistors R need R_f = R/n to give the average?
quiz.a: The output is −(R_f/R)(sum of inputs). The average is (sum)/n. Setting R_f/R = 1/n, that is R_f = R/n, makes the output the negative average.

quiz.q: An inverting summer has R_f = 20 kΩ, v₁ = 0.8 V through R₁ = 10 kΩ, and v₂ = 0.4 V through R₂ = 20 kΩ. Find v_out.
quiz.a: i₁ = 0.8 V / 10 kΩ = 80 µA; i₂ = 0.4 V / 20 kΩ = 20 µA; total = 100 µA. v_out = −100 µA × 20 kΩ = −2 V.

quiz.q: A subtractor has differential gain 1 and uses 1 % resistors. Estimate the worst-case CMRR and the output error for a 5 V common-mode input.
quiz.a: CMRR ≈ 1/(4 × 0.01) = 25, about 28 dB. Common-mode gain is about 1/25 = 0.04. The output error is about 0.04 × 5 V = 0.2 V.

quiz.q: Give two reasons the inverting summer is often preferred over the non-inverting summer.
quiz.a: Its summing node is a true 0 V virtual ground, so the op-amp inputs see no common-mode voltage. Its gain is set by the feedback resistor and input resistors without a signal-dependent divider at the input.

quiz.q: A subtractor has R₁ = 10 kΩ, R_f = 20 kΩ, R₂ = 10 kΩ and R₃ = 20 kΩ. v₁ = 1.2 V and v₂ = 1.8 V. Find v_out.
quiz.a: R₃/R₂ = 2 and R_f/R₁ = 2, so the ratio condition holds. v_out = 2 × (1.8 V − 1.2 V) = 1.2 V.

quiz.q: In a four-resistor subtractor, R₃ is accidentally 10 % high while the other three resistors are exact. Is the common-mode gain zero? Explain.
quiz.a: No. R₃/R₂ no longer equals R_f/R₁, so the two superposition terms do not cancel for a common-mode input. The common-mode gain becomes nonzero and CMRR falls.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, difference amplifiers are built as monolithic resistor-matched blocks or as instrumentation amplifiers, and laser trimming can push CMRR above 80 dB. Switched-capacitor summers are used in sigma-delta ADCs and audio codecs. Search for matched resistor network difference amplifier, weighted resistor DAC, and common-mode rejection ratio resistor mismatch.
